title: Amines and Rearrangements
description: Basicity and synthesis of amines, their characteristic reactions, and rearrangements that move groups to electron-deficient atoms.
overview: Amines are the organic bases. They are in amino acids and proteins, in neurotransmitters such as dopamine and serotonin, in most drugs, and in the alkaloids (morphine, caffeine, nicotine, quinine) that plants make. A nitrogen lone pair makes them basic and nucleophilic, and the same property causes a recurring synthetic problem: an amine is more nucleophilic than the ammonia it came from, so direct alkylation overreacts.

This chapter covers the structure and basicity of amines, the methods that avoid overalkylation, their main reactions, and a family of rearrangements (Hofmann, Curtius, Beckmann, Baeyer–Villiger) in which a group migrates to an electron-deficient nitrogen or oxygen.
objectives: Classify and name amines, and rank them by basicity.
Choose a synthesis of a primary, secondary or tertiary amine that avoids overalkylation.
Predict the products of acylation, exhaustive methylation and Hofmann elimination, and nitrous acid reactions.
Write mechanisms for the Hofmann, Curtius, Beckmann and Baeyer–Villiger rearrangements.
Use migratory aptitude to predict which group moves.

sections.title: Structure, basicity and properties of amines
body: An **amine** has a nitrogen bonded to one, two or three carbons (**primary**, **secondary**, **tertiary**) and a lone pair. Nitrogen is sp³ and pyramidal (C–N–C about 108°). The lone pair undergoes rapid inversion (barrier about 25 kJ mol⁻¹), so an amine with three different groups cannot be resolved. Names: alkanamine (butan-2-amine) or N-substituted names (N-methylpropan-1-amine). A **quaternary ammonium** salt, R₄N⁺, has no lone pair and no inversion.

Amines hydrogen bond through N–H (weaker than O–H), so primary and secondary amines boil between alkanes and alcohols (butylamine 78 °C, butan-1-ol 118 °C, and tertiary amines, with no N–H, lower, like trimethylamine at 3 °C). Low-mass amines dissolve in water. Many amines smell of fish.
The pK_a of the conjugate acid (the **ammonium** ion) measures base strength:

table.caption: Basicity of amines.

body: An amine dissolves in dilute aqueous acid as its ammonium salt, and is recovered with base. This is used to extract amines from organic mixtures, and drugs are often sold as hydrochlorides because the salt is soluble and stable. An aliphatic amine is a weak base but a good nucleophile, and so reacts with alkyl halides, acyl chlorides and carbonyls.

check.q: Why is aniline a much weaker base than cyclohexylamine?
check.a: The nitrogen lone pair is delocalized into the aromatic ring
wrong: The ring donates electrons to nitrogen

sections.title: Synthesis of amines
body: **Direct alkylation** of ammonia or an amine by an alkyl halide gives a mixture, because each product is more nucleophilic than the starting amine: primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary salts all form. It is useful only with a large excess of NH₃, or for making quaternary salts. Better methods give a single class:

head: Method
Starting material
Reagents
Product
rows: Potassium phthalimide (SN2), then N₂H₄ or NaOH
table.caption: Routes to amines.

body: The Gabriel and azide methods work because the nitrogen nucleophile (phthalimide anion, azide) can be alkylated only once, as the product has no remaining nucleophilic N–H or lone pair. Azides are explosive when small and must be handled with care.

check.q: Which method gives a pure primary amine from a primary alkyl bromide?
wrong: Heating with NH₃ in equal amounts

check.q: How are aromatic amines normally made?
check.a: Nitration followed by reduction of the nitro group
wrong: SN2 of NH₃ on aryl halides
Direct amination of benzene with NH₃

sections.title: Reactions of amines

list: **Acylation.** Amines react with acyl chlorides or anhydrides to give amides, which are not basic and cannot be acylated again. Acetylation is used to moderate an aromatic amine’s reactivity (see the chapter on aromatic chemistry).

**Hofmann elimination.** Exhaustive methylation (excess CH₃I) converts an amine to a quaternary ammonium iodide. Ag₂O and water exchange I⁻ for OH⁻, and heating gives an alkene by E2. The leaving group, a tertiary amine, is bulky and poor, and the base removes the most accessible hydrogen. The product is the **less substituted (Hofmann) alkene**, the opposite of Zaitsev. Butan-2-amine gives mainly but-1-ene.

**Hinsberg test.** Benzenesulfonyl chloride reacts with primary amines to give a sulfonamide that dissolves in NaOH (the N–H is acidic), with secondary amines to give an insoluble sulfonamide, and not at all with tertiary amines. It distinguishes the three classes.

**Nitrous acid (NaNO₂, HCl).** Primary aromatic amines give diazonium salts (see the chapter on aromatic chemistry), and primary aliphatic amines give unstable diazonium ions that lose N₂ to give carbocations and mixtures. Secondary amines give **N-nitrosamines** (R₂N–N=O), yellow oils, potent carcinogens formed from amines and nitrite in cured meat and tobacco. Tertiary aliphatic amines are not changed.

body: Many drugs and natural products are amines: the **alkaloids**, nitrogen bases from plants, include morphine, quinine, caffeine, nicotine and cocaine. Their amine groups are protonated at physiological pH, which controls how they cross membranes and bind receptors.

example.title: Hofmann elimination
example.problem: What alkene forms when pentan-2-amine is treated with excess CH₃I, then Ag₂O, then heat?
example.solution: The amine becomes the trimethylammonium hydroxide. E2 removes a β-hydrogen, and the less hindered, more acidic hydrogen is on the methyl (C1), not the CH₂ (C3). The major product is pent-1-ene (Hofmann), with pent-2-ene minor.

check.q: Hofmann elimination of a quaternary ammonium hydroxide gives mainly…
In the Hinsberg test, which amine gives a sulfonamide that dissolves in NaOH?

sections.title: Rearrangements to electron-deficient atoms
body: In several reactions an R group migrates with its bonding pair from carbon to an adjacent electron-deficient nitrogen or oxygen as a leaving group departs. They resemble the carbocation 1,2-shifts but are concerted, with retention of configuration at the migrating carbon.

A primary amide treated with Br₂ and NaOH (**Hofmann rearrangement**) is N-brominated, deprotonated, and the R group migrates from carbon to nitrogen as bromide leaves, giving an **isocyanate** (R–N=C=O), which water hydrolyzes to the amine with loss of CO₂. The product, R–NH₂, has **one carbon fewer** than the amide. The **Curtius rearrangement** reaches the same isocyanate from an **acyl azide** (RCON₃, from an acyl chloride and NaN₃) by heating, with loss of N₂. The isocyanate can be trapped with an alcohol to give a carbamate or with water to give the amine.

A ketone oxime treated with acid rearranges to an amide: the group anti to the leaving OH migrates to nitrogen, giving a nitrilium ion, then the amide. Cyclohexanone oxime gives ε-caprolactam, the monomer of nylon-6, made on a scale of millions of tons per year. The Schmidt reaction of a ketone with HN₃ follows a similar course.

A peroxyacid (mCPBA, peracetic acid) converts a ketone into an ester by inserting oxygen on one side of the carbonyl. The tetrahedral peroxide intermediate (the Criegee intermediate) rearranges as a carboxylate leaves, with one group migrating to oxygen. Cyclic ketones give lactones: cyclohexanone gives ε-caprolactone, a polyester monomer.

When two groups can move, the one best able to stabilize a developing positive charge migrates, giving a general order of **migratory aptitude**: **tertiary alkyl > cyclohexyl > secondary alkyl ≈ phenyl > primary alkyl > methyl**. Hydride also migrates readily. In the Baeyer–Villiger oxidation of 2-methylcyclohexyl methyl ketone, the secondary ring carbon migrates, not the methyl.

example.title: Predicting a Baeyer–Villiger product
example.problem: What does the Baeyer–Villiger oxidation of tert-butyl methyl ketone and of acetophenone with mCPBA give?
example.solution: tert-Butyl methyl ketone: the tertiary group migrates, giving tert-butyl acetate. Acetophenone: phenyl migrates in preference to methyl, giving phenyl acetate.

example.title: Hofmann rearrangement
example.solution: Br₂, NaOH, H₂O: the butyl group migrates to nitrogen, giving butyl isocyanate, which hydrolyzes and loses CO₂. The amine has four carbons, one fewer than the amide.

quiz.q: The nitrogen of ethylmethylpropylamine bears three different groups and a lone pair, yet the amine cannot be resolved into enantiomers at room temperature. Why?
quiz.a: Rapid pyramidal inversion at nitrogen interconverts the enantiomers
wrong: Nitrogen in amines is sp² hybridized and therefore planar, with no stereocenter
The lone pair is not a substituent, so nitrogen has only three groups and cannot be a stereocenter
The C–N bonds rotate freely and average the two mirror-image forms rapidly
quiz.why: The lone pair flips from one face to the other quickly, so the two mirror-image arrangements cannot be separated. A quaternary ammonium ion has no lone pair and no inversion, so it can be resolved.

quiz.q: Trimethylamine boils at 3 °C, but its isomer propylamine boils at 48 °C. The main reason is that
quiz.a: propylamine hydrogen-bonds through its N–H bonds, but trimethylamine has none
wrong: propylamine has the larger molar mass, so its dispersion forces are stronger
trimethylamine is largely ionic in the liquid state, which lowers its boiling point
the lone pair of trimethylamine is sp² hybridized, which weakens intermolecular attraction
quiz.why: Both have the formula C₃H₉N, so mass is the same. Only primary and secondary amines can donate hydrogen bonds through N–H.

quiz.q: Aniline has a conjugate acid pK_a of 4.6. In a buffer at pH 7.6, about what fraction of the aniline is protonated?
quiz.why: [ArNH₃⁺]/[ArNH₂] = 10^(pK_a − pH) = 10^(4.6 − 7.6) = 10⁻³. So essentially all the aniline is the free base at this pH.

quiz.q: Pyridine (conjugate acid pK_a 5.2) is a much weaker base than trimethylamine (9.8). The main reason is that the pyridine lone pair
quiz.a: occupies an sp² orbital, which has more s character and holds the electrons nearer the nucleus
wrong: is delocalized into the aromatic π system, as in aniline, and so is unavailable
is stabilized by hyperconjugation with the neighboring ring carbons, which lowers its energy
is on a nitrogen atom that is sp-hybridized and linear, so protonation is strained
quiz.why: The pyridine lone pair lies in the plane of the ring and is not part of the aromatic sextet. Its sp² orbital binds a proton less readily than the sp³ lone pair of an alkylamine.

quiz.q: A solution of cyclohexylamine and naphthalene in ether is shaken with dilute aqueous HCl. Afterwards the amine is found
quiz.a: in the aqueous layer, as cyclohexylammonium chloride
wrong: in the ether layer, as the free amine, together with the naphthalene
in the ether layer, as an amide formed by reaction with HCl
as a precipitate of the free amine at the interface of the layers
quiz.why: The basic amine is protonated to a water-soluble salt, while neutral naphthalene stays in the ether. Adding base to the aqueous layer later regenerates the amine.

quiz.q: Ethylamine is heated with one equivalent of bromoethane. The product is a mixture of diethylamine, triethylamine and ammonium salts mainly because
quiz.a: each alkylation gives a more nucleophilic amine that competes for the bromoethane
wrong: bromoethane ionizes by SN1 and attacks any nitrogen present in the mixture
the product amine is a weaker base, so it is not protonated and keeps reacting
ethylamine is too hindered to react only once, so a second equivalent is always needed
quiz.why: Alkyl groups donate electron density to nitrogen, so a secondary amine is more nucleophilic than a primary one. Methods such as the Gabriel synthesis avoid this by using a nucleophile that can react only once.
Cyanide adds one carbon, and reduction of the nitrile gives RCH₂NH₂. The Gabriel and azide routes and ammonia give butan-1-amine, with no extra carbon.

quiz.q: The Gabriel synthesis stops cleanly at the primary amine stage because
quiz.a: the N-alkylphthalimide has no N–H and its lone pair is tied up by two carbonyls
wrong: phthalimide anion is too bulky to attack a second molecule of alkyl halide
hydrazine removes any extra alkyl groups from the nitrogen as they are added
the alkyl halide is completely consumed by the first substitution reaction
quiz.why: After one SN2 the nitrogen has no remaining nucleophilic N–H or free lone pair. Only the final hydrazine or NaOH step releases the free primary amine.

quiz.q: Benzoyl chloride is treated with dimethylamine, and the product is then reduced with LiAlH₄. The final product is
wrong: benzyl alcohol, PhCH₂OH, from reduction of the acyl chloride
N-methylbenzylamine, PhCH₂NHCH₃, after loss of one methyl
quiz.why: The acyl chloride gives the tertiary amide, and LiAlH₄ converts C=O to CH₂ in amides to give the amine. The amide is the intermediate, not the product.

quiz.q: In the Hofmann elimination, a quaternary ammonium iodide is treated with Ag₂O and water before heating. What is this step for?
quiz.a: It exchanges iodide for hydroxide, the base for the E2 step
wrong: It reduces the quaternary ammonium ion to the free tertiary amine
It methylates the nitrogen a further time to give a quaternary salt
It oxidizes iodide to iodine, which then serves as the leaving group
quiz.why: Silver iodide precipitates and leaves the ammonium hydroxide, whose OH⁻ removes a β-hydrogen on heating. The leaving group is the neutral tertiary amine.

quiz.q: A sulfonamide made from an unknown amine and benzenesulfonyl chloride does not dissolve in aqueous NaOH. The amine is
quiz.why: A primary amine gives a sulfonamide with an acidic N–H, which dissolves in base. A secondary amine has no N–H left, so its sulfonamide stays insoluble, while a tertiary amine forms no sulfonamide.

quiz.q: Diethylamine is treated with NaNO₂ and HCl. The product is
wrong: diethyldiazonium chloride, which is stable at 0 °C
quiz.why: Secondary amines are nitrosated at nitrogen to give N-nitrosamines, R₂N–N=O, which are potent carcinogens. Only primary amines can form diazonium ions.

quiz.q: (S)-2-Methylbutanamide is treated with Br₂ and NaOH. The product is
quiz.why: The migrating carbon keeps its configuration, and the NH₂ takes the place of the CONH₂ in the same priority position. The product has one carbon fewer than the amide.

quiz.q: An acyl azide RCON₃ is heated in ethanol. The final product is
quiz.why: Heating causes the Curtius rearrangement to an isocyanate, R–N=C=O, with loss of N₂. Ethanol traps it as the carbamate, whereas water would give the amine.

quiz.q: Cyclopentanone oxime is treated with H₂SO₄. The main product is
quiz.why: In the Beckmann rearrangement a ring carbon migrates to nitrogen, inserting N into the ring. A five-membered ring becomes a six-membered one, as cyclohexanone gives caprolactam.

quiz.q: Propiophenone, PhCOCH₂CH₃, is treated with mCPBA. The product is
quiz.why: Phenyl has a higher migratory aptitude than a primary alkyl group, so phenyl moves to oxygen. The ethyl group stays on the carbonyl carbon, giving PhO–CO–CH₂CH₃.

summary: Amines are basic (ammonium pK_a about 10–11) and nucleophilic. Aromatic amines and amides are far less basic.
Avoid overalkylation by using azide, Gabriel, nitrile or amide reduction, reductive amination, or nitro reduction.
Hofmann elimination gives the less substituted alkene. The Hinsberg test separates 1°, 2° and 3° amines. Secondary amines form nitrosamines with nitrite.
Hofmann and Curtius rearrangements convert acids and amides to amines with one fewer carbon through isocyanates.
Beckmann converts oximes to amides (caprolactam). Baeyer–Villiger converts ketones to esters. Migratory aptitude: 3° > cyclohexyl > 2° ≈ phenyl > 1° > methyl.

problems.q: Propose syntheses of (a) benzylamine from benzyl bromide, (b) N-ethylaniline from aniline, (c) 2-phenylethylamine from benzyl bromide.
problems.solution: (a) Potassium phthalimide, then hydrazine (Gabriel), or NaN₃ then LiAlH₄. (b) Acetylate aniline, reduce with LiAlH₄ to N-ethylaniline; or react aniline with acetaldehyde and NaBH₃CN. (c) NaCN (SN2) to benzyl cyanide, then LiAlH₄ reduces the nitrile to PhCH₂CH₂NH₂.
problems.a: (a) Gabriel or azide route; (b) acylation then LiAlH₄, or reductive amination; (c) NaCN then LiAlH₄.

problems.q: Give the structure of the product of (a) cyclopentanone + mCPBA, (b) benzamide + Br₂/NaOH, (c) the oxime of acetophenone + H₂SO₄ (phenyl migrates).
Rank by basicity: ethylamine, aniline, acetamide, ammonia, pyridine.
